core_obligations: Monomorphisms (proof lines 381-403): a map is injective if and only if it is a monomorphism; the forward implication is straightforward, and for the converse the author replaces two elements with equal images by the corresponding natural transformations from the representable presheaf, so that monicity gives equality of the transformations and hence of the elements.

Epimorphisms (proof lines 406-442): a map is surjective if and only if it is an epimorphism; the forward implication is straightforward, and for the converse the author forms the presheaf of pushouts of each value along its component, exhibits the two canonical natural transformations from the target into it, uses that these agree after precomposition with the given map and hence, by the epimorphism property, agree everywhere, and concludes that every component is surjective by the set-theoretic characterization of surjectivity through its own pushout.

Isomorphisms (proof lines 445-453): a map is an isomorphism if and only if it is both injective and surjective; again one direction is straightforward, and for the other the pointwise inverses are combined into a natural transformation which is a two-sided inverse.
proof_roadmap: Compare injectivity with the monomorphism property using the Yoneda identification of elements with maps from representables.
Compare surjectivity with the epimorphism property using the presheaf of pushouts along the components.
Combine the two pointwise criteria into the characterization of isomorphisms.
difficulty_reason: The lemma identifies the injective and surjective maps of presheaves of sets, as defined componentwise, with the monomorphisms and epimorphisms of the category of presheaves, and characterizes isomorphisms as the maps that are both (statement lines 372-378). The proof is a complete argument in three parts: injectivity is compared with monicity through the Yoneda identification of elements with natural transformations from representables (proof lines 381-403); surjectivity is compared with the epimorphism property by constructing the presheaf of pushouts along the components and using the two canonical maps into it (proof lines 406-442); and the characterization of isomorphisms is obtained by combining pointwise inverses into a natural transformation (proof lines 445-453). The non-formal content is the pushout construction in the second part and the Yoneda translation in the first. The claim is H2: three written-out equivalences with each input named.
